headline: Medicare open enrollment calls
tip: Medicare open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7, and scammers know it. Medicare won't call you to sell a plan or ask for your Medicare number.

example.title: "Your Medicare Plan Is Changing"
example.subject: Phone call
example.body: "Hello! It's open enrollment season, and your current Medicare plan is being discontinued. I can switch you to a better plan with extra dental and vision at no cost today. I'll just need to confirm your Medicare number and your Social Security number."
redFlags: Asks for your Medicare and Social Security numbers
Claims your plan is being "discontinued" to scare you
example.explanation: Medicare doesn't call you to sell plans or ask for your numbers. Real plan changes come in the mail, in your Annual Notice of Change.
example.howToSpot: Hang up. To compare plans, call 1-800-MEDICARE or visit medicare.gov, or talk to your local SHIP counselor (free Medicare help).

headline: Fake jury duty calls
tip: Courts usually contact jurors by mail. They don't call to demand a fine for missing jury duty.

example.title: "You Missed Jury Duty"
example.subject: Phone call
example.body: "This is Deputy Harris with the County Sheriff's Office. You failed to appear for jury duty and a warrant has been issued for your arrest. You can resolve this today by paying a $1,200 fine. Stay on the line and I'll tell you how to pay with prepaid cards."
redFlags: A fine paid by phone with prepaid cards
Told to stay on the line
example.explanation: Courts and sheriffs don't call to collect fines for missed jury duty, and they never take prepaid or gift cards.
example.howToSpot: Hang up. Look up your local court's number yourself and call to ask.

headline: "Your package is on hold" texts
tip: Package texts surge as holiday shopping begins. Check deliveries in the store's app or on the shipper's real website, never through a text link.

example.title: Delivery "Address Problem" Text
example.subject: Text Message
example.body: USPS: Your package is on hold due to an incomplete address. Please update your details within 12 hours or it will be returned: usps-redeliver-help.com
example.explanation: The fake site asks for your address, then a small "redelivery fee" to capture your card number.
example.howToSpot: Don't tap the link. Track packages using the tracking number from the store you ordered from, or at usps.com. Forward the text to 7726.

headline: A real bank alert, for comparison
tip: Not every message is a scam. Real alerts don't ask for passwords or codes, and you can always check by calling the number on your card.

example.title: Low Balance Alert You Signed Up For
example.subject: Text Message
example.body: First National: Your checking account ending in 4821 is below your $100 alert amount. No reply needed. To manage alerts, open the First National app.
example.explanation: This is a normal alert: it comes from the same number as your other bank alerts, it shows only the last four digits, there's no link, and it tells you to use the bank's own app.
example.howToSpot: Even with real alerts, check your account by opening the bank's app yourself or calling the number on your card.

headline: Charity scams after disasters
tip: After hurricanes and fires, fake charities appear overnight. Give to groups you already know, through their own website.

example.title: Urgent Hurricane Relief Call
example.subject: Phone call
example.body: "Families are sleeping in their cars tonight after the hurricane. Can we count on you for $100? We need to get supplies out today. The fastest way to help is a gift card. Just read me the numbers and I'll make sure it gets to a family."
redFlags: A charity you've never heard of
example.explanation: Real charities never ask for gift cards, and they're happy to let you give later through their website.
example.howToSpot: Say "I'll give through your website," then hang up. Check charities at give.org or charitynavigator.org before donating.

headline: QR code parking tickets
tip: Scammers put fake QR code stickers on parking meters and fake tickets on windshields. Pay through the official parking app or the city's website.

example.title: Ticket on Your Windshield with a QR Code
example.sender: Paper notice under your windshield wiper
example.subject: PARKING VIOLATION NOTICE
example.body:
PARKING VIOLATION — Expired meter
Fine: $45.00
Pay within 24 hours to avoid a $150 late penalty.

Scan the QR code below to pay now.
[QR code]
redFlags: No city name, officer, or citation number you can check
example.explanation: The QR code leads to a fake payment page that steals your card number.
example.howToSpot: Look up your city's parking office yourself to check any ticket. Don't scan QR codes on stickers or notices you weren't expecting.

headline: Too-good holiday deals
tip: Fake online stores pop up before Black Friday with huge discounts. Shop at stores you know, and pay with a credit card.

example.title: 80% Off Name-Brand Shoes
example.subject: Facebook ad
example.body: 🔥 BLACK FRIDAY CLEARANCE 🔥 Store closing! All name-brand walking shoes 80% OFF — only $19.99. Limited stock, sale ends tonight! Shop now at comfy-shoes-outlet.shop
redFlags: Prices far too good to be true
A web address you've never heard of
example.explanation: Fake stores take your payment and send nothing, or send cheap knockoffs. Some also save your card number.
example.howToSpot: Type the brand's real website yourself. Pay with a credit card so you can dispute the charge.

headline: Gift card "help" from the boss or pastor
tip: Scammers pretend to be someone you know, like a pastor, a boss, or a club leader, and ask you to buy gift cards as a favor.

example.title: "Can You Do Me a Quick Favor?"
example.subject: Quick favor
example.body: Hi, are you available? I'm in a meeting and can't talk on the phone. I need to get some gift cards for a few church members who are going through a hard time. Can you pick up 4 Apple gift cards at $100 each? Send me photos of the backs and I'll pay you back on Sunday. Please keep this between us for now.
redFlags: Asks for gift cards and photos of the backs
A Gmail address instead of the church's usual email
example.explanation: Scammers copy the names of people you trust. Once you send photos of the card numbers, the money is gone.
example.howToSpot: Call the person on a number you already have. A real pastor or boss will never mind you checking.
